books.title: The Return of Sherlock Holmes
books.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
books.desc: Sherlock Holmes, believed dead at the Reichenbach Falls, returns to Baker Street for thirteen new cases.
about: Three years after the fatal struggle with Professor Moriarty, Dr Watson is investigating the strange murder of the Honourable Ronald Adair in London when Sherlock Holmes reappears, alive, and explains his disappearance. The two friends resume their partnership, and the following stories take them from a cipher of dancing stick figures to a blackmailer of high society, from a series of smashed busts of Napoleon to a missing rugby player and a stolen diplomatic letter.
These thirteen stories continue to combine Holmes's powers of observation and deduction with vivid portraits of Victorian and Edwardian society, seen through the eyes of the loyal Watson.

The stories were first published in The Strand Magazine in Britain and Collier's in the United States between 1903 and 1904, and were collected in book form in 1905. They include "The Empty House", "The Dancing Men", "Charles Augustus Milverton", "The Six Napoleons" and "The Second Stain".

books.title: The Duchess of Malfi
books.author: John Webster
books.desc: A young widowed duchess secretly marries her steward against the will of her brothers, who set a spy to watch her.
about: The young Duchess of Malfi, a widow, is forbidden by her brothers, Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria, and the Cardinal, to marry again. Ferdinand places Bosola, a discontented former galley-slave, in her household as a spy. Defying them, the Duchess secretly marries Antonio, her honest steward, with only her maid Cariola as witness, and has children by him. When Bosola discovers the secret, the brothers' fury sets the tragedy in motion.

Webster's play is a dark Jacobean tragedy of corruption, cruelty and madness, set in the courts of Italy. Its heroine's courage and dignity in suffering, and its intense, often violent poetry, are among its most remarked features.
The Duchess of Malfi was first performed in 1613 or 1614 by the King's Men, Shakespeare's company, at the Blackfriars Theatre and at the Globe. It was printed in quarto in 1623.
books.author_short: English Jacobean dramatist (c. 1580–c. 1634), author of the tragedies The White Devil and The Duchess of Malfi.
author_long: Little is known for certain about John Webster's life. He was born in London around 1580 into a merchant family, probably studied at Merchant Taylors' School, and died around 1634.

His most famous plays are the tragedies The White Devil (1612) and The Duchess of Malfi (1613–1614). He also wrote The Devil's Law-Case and worked with other playwrights, among them Thomas Dekker, with whom he wrote Westward Ho.

books.title: The Water-Babies
books.author: Charles Kingsley
books.desc: Tom, a little chimney sweep, falls into a river, becomes a water-baby and sets off on a moral journey through rivers and seas.
about: Tom is a poor, ignorant chimney sweep who works for the brutal master sweep Grimes. Sent to clean the chimneys of Harthover Place, the house of Sir John, he loses his way in the flues and comes out in the bedroom of the little girl Ellie. Chased away as a thief, he flees across the moors and falls into a river, where he is transformed into a water-baby. Under the guidance of the fairies Mrs Bedonebyasyoudid and Mrs Doasyouwouldbedoneby, he must learn to become good.

Kingsley's fantasy mixes adventure, natural history, moral lessons and satire, including comments on the scientific debates that followed Darwin's On the Origin of Species and a protest against the use of young children as chimney sweeps. Some passages contain disparaging remarks about the Irish and other peoples that reflect prejudices of its time.
The Water-Babies was written as a serial for Macmillan's Magazine in 1862 and 1863, and was published as a book in 1863.
books.author_short: English clergyman, novelist and social reformer (1819–1875), author of Westward Ho! and The Water-Babies.
author_long: Charles Kingsley was born on 12 June 1819 at Holne in Devon. A clergyman of the Church of England, he became the parish clergyman of Eversley in Hampshire in 1844 and spent much of his life there. A supporter of Christian socialism, he was concerned with the condition of the poor. In 1860 he was appointed Regius Professor of Modern History at Cambridge. He died at Eversley on 23 January 1875.
His novels include Westward Ho! (1855) and Hereward the Wake (1866), and his best-known book for children is The Water-Babies (1863).

books.title: Utopia
books.author: Thomas More
books.desc: A traveller describes to Thomas More a distant island whose people share all their goods and live by reason, in contrast to the injustices of Europe.
about: While on a diplomatic mission in Flanders, Thomas More meets his friend Peter Giles in Antwerp, who introduces him to Raphael Hythloday, a Portuguese traveller who has sailed with Amerigo Vespucci. In the first part, Hythloday criticises the injustices of England and Europe, such as the hanging of thieves driven to crime by poverty. In the second, he describes the island of Utopia, its capital Amaurot, and the customs of its people, who hold all property in common, work six hours a day, choose their magistrates and tolerate different religions.

More's dialogue is at once a serious work of political philosophy and a playful fiction; the name Utopia, from the Greek, means "no place". It raises lasting questions about property, justice, work and government, though Utopian society also includes slavery and strict control over its citizens' lives.

Utopia was written in Latin and first printed at Louvain in 1516, with the help of Erasmus and Peter Giles. It was first published in English in 1551 in the translation by Ralph Robinson. This edition reproduces the translation by Gilbert Burnet, published in 1684.
books.author_short: English lawyer, humanist and statesman (1478–1535), author of Utopia, executed for refusing to recognise Henry VIII as head of the Church.
author_long: Thomas More was born in London on 7 February 1478. A lawyer and a friend of Erasmus, he entered the service of Henry VIII and served as Lord Chancellor from 1529 to 1532. In 1534 he refused to swear the oath accepting the king's authority over the Church, was imprisoned in the Tower of London, and was beheaded as a traitor on 6 July 1535.
His most famous work is Utopia (1516). He was canonised by the Catholic Church in 1935.

books.title: Allan Quatermain
books.author: H. Rider Haggard
books.desc: Grieving the death of his son, the old hunter Allan Quatermain sets off with his friends to find a lost civilisation in the heart of Africa.
about: After the death of his only son, Allan Quatermain cannot bear life in England and persuades his friends Sir Henry Curtis and Captain John Good to return with him to Africa, in search of a rumoured people living beyond the unexplored mountains. They are joined by the old Zulu warrior Umslopogaas and, later, by the comic French cook Alphonse. After a battle at the mission station of Mr Mackenzie, they reach the hidden kingdom of the Zu-Vendi, ruled by two rival queens, Nyleptha and Sorais.

This sequel to King Solomon's Mines combines battles, journeys and romance. Its presentation of Africa and Africans, and its idea of a hidden white civilisation, reflect the colonial and racial attitudes of its time.
Allan Quatermain was serialised in Longman's Magazine from January to August 1887 and published as a book the same year.
